    00.0 Welcome to Arrays
Imagine you have a collection of your favorite books, a list of daily temperatures, or a set of scores from your last game. How do you keep track of all these pieces of information efficiently in your code? The answer lies in arrays — one of the most fundamental tools in programming.
What Are Arrays?
An array is like a container that holds multiple values under a single name. Instead of creating separate variables for each item, arrays let you group related data together in an ordered list. Each item in an array has a specific position, called an index, starting at 0.
For example, instead of having:
typescriptlet grade1 = 85;
let grade2 = 90;
let grade3 = 78;

You can use an array:
typescriptlet grades = [85, 90, 78];

Here, grades[0] is 85, grades[1] is 90, and so on.
Why Are Arrays Important?
Arrays help you:

Organize data efficiently: Manage lists of items without cluttering your code.
Process data easily: Perform operations on all elements using loops and methods.
Solve real-world problems: From shopping carts to game boards, arrays model collections naturally.

Connecting to What You Know
You've learned about variables and functions before. Arrays build on these concepts by grouping multiple values, and functions will help you manipulate these groups effectively.
What to Expect in This Course
You'll start by learning how to create and access arrays, then move on to adding and removing elements. You'll explore essential array methods, iteration techniques, and even multi-dimensional arrays called matrices. Finally, you'll master searching and sorting algorithms to handle data like a pro.
Visualizing Arrays

This illustration shows an array as a sequence of boxes, each holding a value and labeled with its index starting from 0.
Ready to Dive In?
Understanding arrays opens the door to powerful programming techniques. As you progress, you'll see how arrays make your code cleaner, faster, and more flexible.
Let's embark on this journey to master arrays and unlock new possibilities in your coding adventure!

    01.0 Understanding Arrays
Arrays are one of the most powerful tools in programming for managing collections of data efficiently. In this lesson, we'll explore what arrays are, how they are structured in TypeScript, and why they are essential for organizing multiple related values under a single variable.
What Is an Array?
An array is an ordered collection of elements, all stored under one variable name. Instead of creating separate variables for each item, arrays let you group related data together in a list where each element has a specific position called an index.
Key Characteristics of Arrays:

Ordered: Elements are stored in a sequence.
Indexed: Each element has a zero-based index (the first element is at index 0).
Homogeneous: In TypeScript, arrays typically contain elements of the same type.

Why Use Arrays Instead of Individual Variables?
Imagine you want to store the names of three students:
typescriptlet student1 = "Ana";
let student2 = "Carlos";
let student3 = "Maria";

This approach quickly becomes cumbersome as the number of items grows. Instead, using an array:
typescriptlet students: string[] = ["Ana", "Carlos", "Maria"];

This way, you can manage all student names under one variable, making your code cleaner and easier to maintain.
Array Syntax in TypeScript

Declaration: Use square brackets [] to denote an array type.

typescriptlet numbers: number[] = [10, 20, 30];
let flags: boolean[] = [true, false, true];


Accessing Elements: Use bracket notation with the index.

typescriptconsole.log(numbers[0]); // Outputs: 10


Zero-Based Indexing: The first element is at index 0, the second at 1, and so on.

The .length Property
Every array has a .length property that tells you how many elements it contains.
typescriptconsole.log(students.length); // Outputs: 3

This is useful for loops and dynamic operations.
When to Use Arrays
Use arrays when you need to:

Store multiple related values.
Perform operations on collections of data.
Manage data that can grow or shrink dynamically.

Summary

Arrays group multiple values under one name.
Elements are accessed by zero-based indices.
TypeScript arrays should contain elements of the same type.
The .length property helps manage array size.

Example: Accessing Array Elements
typescriptlet fruits: string[] = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];
console.log(fruits[1]); // Outputs: banana

Your Turn!
In your own words, explain what an array is and why it is useful in programming.

This question encourages you to reflect and articulate your understanding, reinforcing the core concepts of arrays.

Keep practicing creating and accessing arrays to build a strong foundation for more advanced data manipulation techniques ahead!

    InstructionsCode01.1 Creating and Accessing Arrays
In programming, arrays are your go-to tool for storing multiple related values under a single variable name. In this lesson, you'll learn how to create arrays in TypeScript using literal notation and type annotations, access their elements, modify values, and safely handle array indices.
Creating Arrays with Literal Notation and Type Annotations
In TypeScript, you can create arrays by listing elements inside square brackets []. To ensure type safety, you specify the type of elements the array will hold using type annotations.
typescript// Array of strings representing tweets
let twitterFeed: string[] = ["Tweet1", "Tweet2", "Tweet3"];

// Array of numbers representing likes
let instagramLikes: number[] = [120, 340, 560];

// Array of booleans representing user activity
let isActive: boolean[] = [true, false, true];

Here, twitterFeed is an array of strings, instagramLikes holds numbers, and isActive contains boolean values.
Accessing Array Elements
You access elements in an array using bracket notation with the element's index inside the brackets. Remember, arrays are zero-indexed, so the first element is at index 0.
typescriptconsole.log(twitterFeed[0]); // Outputs: "Tweet1" (first tweet)
console.log(instagramLikes[2]); // Outputs: 560 (likes on third post)
console.log(isActive[1]); // Outputs: false (second user's activity status)

Modifying Array Elements
You can change the value of an element by assigning a new value to a specific index.
typescripttwitterFeed[1] = "Updated Tweet"; // Change second tweet
instagramLikes[0] = 150; // Update likes on first post
isActive[2] = false; // Change third user's activity status

Using the .length Property
The .length property tells you how many elements are in the array. This is useful for loops and dynamic operations.
typescriptconsole.log(`Number of tweets: ${twitterFeed.length}`); // Outputs: Number of tweets: 3

Safe Access: Avoiding Out-of-Bounds Errors
Accessing an index outside the array returns undefined. To avoid unexpected results, always check if the index is within bounds.
typescriptconsole.log(twitterFeed[10]); // undefined

let index = 2;
if (index >= 0 && index < twitterFeed.length) {
  console.log(twitterFeed[index]);
} else {
  console.log("Index out of bounds");
}

Summary

Use literal notation [] with type annotations to create arrays.
Access elements with bracket notation using zero-based indices.
Modify elements by assigning new values to specific indices.
Use the .length property to get the array size.
Always check index bounds before accessing elements to avoid undefined.

Try the following coding challenge to apply what you've learned about creating and accessing arrays.

Keep experimenting with arrays to build a strong foundation for more advanced data manipulation techniques coming up next!123456789101112131415// Create an array called favoriteSongs with 5 song titleslet favoriteSongs: string[] = ["Song1", "Song2", "Song3", "Song4", "Song5"];// Print the first songconsole.log(favoriteSongs[0]);// Print the last songconsole.log(favoriteSongs[4]);// Change the third song to a new titlefavoriteSongs[2] = "New Song";// Print the updated arrayconsole.log(favoriteSongs);Read the instructions and fill in your code to complete the exercise.

    InstructionsCode01.2 Adding and Removing Elements
Managing collections of data often requires dynamically adding or removing items. In this lesson, you'll learn how to modify arrays in TypeScript using four essential methods: push, unshift, pop, and shift. These methods let you add or remove elements from the beginning or end of an array, changing its size and order.
Adding Elements

.push(element) adds an element to the end of the array.
.unshift(element) adds an element to the beginning of the array.

Both methods mutate the original array and increase its length.
typescriptlet supportQueue: string[] = [];

supportQueue.push("Alice"); // Queue: ["Alice"]
supportQueue.push("Bob");   // Queue: ["Alice", "Bob"]

supportQueue.unshift("VIP_Charlie"); // Queue: ["VIP_Charlie", "Alice", "Bob"]

console.log(supportQueue); // Outputs: ["VIP_Charlie", "Alice", "Bob"]

Removing Elements

.pop() removes and returns the element from the end of the array.
.shift() removes and returns the element from the beginning of the array.

These methods mutate the array and decrease its length.
typescriptlet servedUser = supportQueue.shift();
console.log(`Served: ${servedUser}`); // "VIP_Charlie"
console.log(supportQueue); // ["Alice", "Bob"]

let leftUser = supportQueue.pop();
console.log(`Left queue: ${leftUser}`); // "Bob"
console.log(supportQueue); // ["Alice"]

Important Notes

These methods change the original array (mutation).
push and unshift add elements; pop and shift remove elements.
pop and shift return the removed element, which can be stored or logged.
The array's length property updates automatically.

Real-World Example: Queue Management
Imagine managing a customer support queue where new customers join at the end, but VIP customers get priority at the front. When a customer is served, they leave the front of the queue, and sometimes customers leave from the end.
This pattern models many real-world scenarios like social media feeds, task scheduling, or event management.
Summary

Use .push() to add elements at the end.
Use .unshift() to add elements at the beginning.
Use .pop() to remove elements from the end.
Use .shift() to remove elements from the beginning.
These methods modify the array and affect its length.


Practice Challenge: Build a Queue System
Practice Challenge: Build a Queue System
In this challenge, you will create a simple queue management system using TypeScript arrays. Your task is to:

Initialize an empty queue to hold customer names.
Add new customers to the end of the queue using .push().
Add VIP customers to the front of the queue using .unshift().
Remove customers from the front of the queue when they are served using .shift().
Remove customers from the end of the queue if they leave early using .pop().

Make sure to log the state of the queue after each operation to verify your implementation. Experiment with different sequences of adding and removing customers to see how the queue changes dynamically.
Good luck and have fun managing your queue!

Keep experimenting with these methods to see how arrays can model dynamic data structures effectively!12345678910111213141516171819202122232425// Queue system simulation using arrays in TypeScriptlet queue: string[] = [];// Function to add a customer to the end of the queuefunction addCustomer(name: string) {  // TODO: add the customer to the end of the queue}// Function to add a VIP customer to the front of the queuefunction addVIPCustomer(name: string) {  // TODO: add the VIP customer to the front of the queue}// Function to serve the next customer (remove from front)function serveCustomer(): string | undefined {  // TODO: remove and return the customer at the front of the queue  return undefined;}// Function to remove the last customer who left the queuefunction removeLastCustomer(): string | undefined {  // TODO: remove and return the customer at the end of the queue  return undefined;}Read the instructions and fill in your code to complete the exercise.

    01.3 Essential Array Methods
Arrays in TypeScript come with powerful properties and methods that help you manage and query data efficiently. In this lesson, we'll explore some of the most commonly used array features: .length, .indexOf(), .includes(), .slice(), and .concat(). Understanding these will make your code cleaner, more readable, and less error-prone.

The .length Property
Every array has a .length property that tells you how many elements it contains. This is especially useful for loops and dynamic operations.
typescriptlet fruits: string[] = ["apple", "banana", "orange", "banana"];
console.log(`Total fruits: ${fruits.length}`); // Outputs: 4

Remember, .length always reflects the current number of elements, even after adding or removing items.

Finding Elements: .indexOf() and .includes()
.indexOf()

Returns the first index where a specified element is found.
Returns -1 if the element is not present.

typescriptlet firstBananaIndex = fruits.indexOf("banana");
console.log(`First banana at index: ${firstBananaIndex}`); // 1

let grapeIndex = fruits.indexOf("grape");
console.log(`Grape found? ${grapeIndex !== -1}`); // false

.includes()

Returns a boolean indicating whether the array contains the element.

typescriptlet hasOrange = fruits.includes("orange");
console.log(`Contains orange? ${hasOrange}`); // true

Use .includes() when you only need to check presence, and .indexOf() when you need the position.

Extracting Portions: .slice()
The .slice() method creates a new array by extracting a portion of an existing array without modifying the original.

Syntax: array.slice(startIndex, endIndex)
Extracts elements from startIndex up to but not including endIndex.

typescriptlet citrus = fruits.slice(2, 4); // Elements at indices 2 and 3
console.log(citrus); // ["orange", "banana"]

// Preview first 3 items
let preview = fruits.slice(0, 3);
console.log(preview); // ["apple", "banana", "orange"]

This is useful for pagination, previews, or working with subsets of data.

Combining Arrays: .concat()
The .concat() method merges two or more arrays into a new array without changing the originals.
typescriptlet moreFruits = ["mango", "pineapple"];
let allFruits = fruits.concat(moreFruits);
console.log(allFruits); // ["apple", "banana", "orange", "banana", "mango", "pineapple"]

This method is great for combining data from multiple sources, like merging lists of items or tags.

Mutating vs Non-Mutating Methods

Methods like .push() and .pop() change the original array (mutate).
Methods like .slice() and .concat() return new arrays and do not mutate the original.

Understanding this difference helps avoid unintended side effects in your programs.

Conceptual Illustration


Summary

Use .length to get the number of elements.
Use .indexOf() to find the first position of an element.
Use .includes() to check if an element exists.
Use .slice() to extract parts of an array without changing it.
Use .concat() to merge arrays into a new one.
Know which methods mutate the original array and which do not.


Reflective Question
In your own words, explain the difference between mutating and non-mutating array methods and why it is important to understand this distinction.


Keep experimenting with these methods on your own arrays to see how they behave and when to use each effectively!

    InstructionsCode02.0 Looping Through Arrays
Iteration is the key that unlocks the full potential of arrays, allowing you to process and manipulate data with precision and flexibility. Now that you understand how to use for and while loops effectively, you can traverse any collection, whether you're counting items, searching for values, or performing calculations. This skill transforms arrays from static lists into dynamic tools that respond to your program's needs.
Why Iterate Through Arrays?
Arrays store multiple elements, but to work with each element, you need to visit them one by one. This process is called iteration. Iteration lets you:

Access every element in order
Perform operations like summing values or finding the maximum
Search for specific items
Modify elements based on conditions

Without iteration, you'd have to access each element manually, which is impractical and error-prone.
The For Loop: Index-Based Traversal
The for loop is the most common way to iterate through arrays when you know the number of elements.
typescriptlet numbers: number[] = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];

for (let i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {
  console.log(`Element at index ${i} is ${numbers[i]}`);
}


Initialization: let i = 0 starts the index at 0 (arrays are zero-based).
Condition: i < numbers.length ensures the loop runs while i is less than the array length.
Increment: i++ increases the index by 1 each iteration.

This loop visits each element in order, giving you access to both the element and its index.
The While Loop: Condition-Based Iteration
The while loop runs as long as a condition is true. It's useful when you don't know in advance how many times you'll iterate.
typescriptlet i = 0;
let total = 0;
let numbers: number[] = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];

while (i < numbers.length && total < 100) {
  total += numbers[i];
  i++;
}

console.log(`Total sum until limit reached: ${total}`);

Here, the loop adds numbers until the total reaches 100 or all elements are processed.
When to Use Each Loop?

Use for loops when you need to iterate a known number of times or access indices.
Use while loops when iteration depends on a condition that may change dynamically.

Both loops are powerful tools for array processing.
Summary

Iteration lets you process each element in an array.
For loops are index-based and great for fixed-length arrays.
While loops run based on conditions and are flexible.
Mastering iteration unlocks advanced data manipulation and problem-solving.

Ready to Practice?
Try applying these loops to real arrays and see how you can count, search, and calculate with ease!12345678910111213141516171819// Define an array of daily temperaturesconst temperatures = [23, 25, 22, 20, 26, 28, 24];// Use a for loop to print each temperature with its day numberfor (let i = 1; i <= temperatures.length; i++) {  console.log(`Day ${i}: Temperature is ${temperatures[i]}`);}// Use a while loop to calculate the total temperature until the sum exceeds 100let totalTemp = 0;let day = 0;while (totalTemp < 100) {  totalTemp += temperatures[day];  day++;}// Print the number of days processed in the while loopconsole.log(`Number of days processed: ${day}`);Read the instructions and fill in your code to complete the exercise.

    02.1 Modern Iteration Methods
In the world of TypeScript, modern array methods like .forEach(), .map(), and .filter() provide powerful, readable ways to process and transform data collections. These methods help you write concise, declarative code that replaces verbose loops, making your programs easier to understand and maintain.
Exploring the Methods
1. .forEach(): Execute a Function for Each Element
The .forEach() method runs a provided function once for every element in the array. It’s perfect for performing side effects like printing or logging values.
typescriptconst grades: number[] = [72, 85, 90, 66, 88];
grades.forEach((grade, index) => {
  console.log(`Student ${index + 1} scored: ${grade}`);
});

This prints each student's grade with their number. Note that .forEach() does not return a new array; it simply executes the function.
2. .map(): Transform Each Element into a New Array
Use .map() when you want to create a new array by transforming each element of the original array.
typescript// Boost each grade by 5 points, capped at 100
const boostedGrades = grades.map(grade => Math.min(grade + 5, 100));
console.log('Boosted Grades:', boostedGrades);

Here, .map() returns a new array where each grade is increased by 5, but not exceeding 100.
3. .filter(): Select Elements That Meet a Condition
The .filter() method creates a new array containing only elements that satisfy a given condition.
typescript// Filter passing grades (70 or higher)
const passingGrades = boostedGrades.filter(grade => grade >= 70);
console.log('Passing Grades:', passingGrades);

This filters out grades below 70, leaving only passing scores.
Combining Methods for Powerful Data Processing
You can chain these methods to perform multiple operations in a clean, readable way.
typescriptboostedGrades
  .filter(grade => grade >= 70)
  .forEach((grade, idx) => console.log(`Passing student ${idx + 1}: ${grade}`));

This boosts grades, filters passing ones, and prints each passing student's grade.
Why Use These Methods?

They replace complex loops with simple, declarative code.
They help avoid common loop pitfalls like off-by-one errors.
They are widely used in real-world applications, from filtering social media posts to transforming playlists.
They encourage immutability by returning new arrays instead of modifying the original.

Try It Yourself!
Experiment with these methods by:

Changing the boost value in .map() and observing the results.
Adjusting the passing threshold in .filter().
Using .map() to convert numeric grades to letter grades (A, B, C, etc.).

These exercises will deepen your understanding and prepare you for more advanced data manipulation.

    02.2 Practical Iteration Patterns
In programming, iteration is the process of visiting each element in a collection to perform operations like finding values, calculating totals, or counting specific items. These patterns are essential for analyzing data and building useful insights.
Let's explore some common iteration tasks using a shopping cart example, where we have an array of product prices:
typescriptconst cart: number[] = [15.99, 23.5, 9.99, 45.0, 12.75, 7.5];

1. Finding the Most Expensive Item (Maximum Value)
To find the highest price, we start by assuming the first item is the most expensive, then compare it with each subsequent item:
typescriptlet maxPrice = cart[0];
for (let i = 1; i < cart.length; i++) {
  if (cart[i] > maxPrice) {
    maxPrice = cart[i];
  }
}
console.log(`Most expensive item: $${maxPrice.toFixed(2)}`);

This loop checks each price and updates maxPrice when a higher value is found.
2. Finding the Cheapest Item (Minimum Value)
Similarly, to find the lowest price:
typescriptlet minPrice = cart[0];
for (let i = 1; i < cart.length; i++) {
  if (cart[i] < minPrice) {
    minPrice = cart[i];
  }
}
console.log(`Cheapest item: $${minPrice.toFixed(2)}`);

3. Calculating the Total Cost (Sum)
Summing all prices gives the total cost:
typescriptlet totalCost = 0;
for (const price of cart) {
  totalCost += price;
}
console.log(`Total cost: $${totalCost.toFixed(2)}`);

4. Counting Items Above a Threshold
To count how many items cost more than $10:
typescriptlet countAboveTen = 0;
for (const price of cart) {
  if (price > 10) {
    countAboveTen++;
  }
}
console.log(`Items costing more than $10: ${countAboveTen}`);

5. Creating a New Array with Discounted Prices
Using the .map() method, we can create a new array with each price discounted by 10%:
typescriptconst discountedPrices = cart.map(price => price * 0.9);
console.log('Discounted prices:', discountedPrices.map(p => `$${p.toFixed(2)}`));

This does not modify the original array but returns a new one with transformed values.

Why These Patterns Matter

Finding max/min helps identify extremes in data.
Summing is fundamental for totals and averages.
Counting supports filtering and statistics.
Mapping transforms data efficiently.

Mastering these iteration patterns equips you to analyze and manipulate data collections effectively.

Reflect and Explain
How would you explain the difference between using a traditional for loop and the .map() method for processing arrays? What are the advantages and scenarios where each is preferable?


Keep practicing these iteration patterns by modifying the cart array or applying similar logic to other datasets. Understanding these basics will prepare you for more advanced data manipulation and algorithms ahead!

    03.1 Working with Matrices
In this lesson, you'll learn how to create, modify, and expand matrices in TypeScript by building a movie theater seating system. This practical example will help you understand how to work with multi-dimensional arrays programmatically.
Creating a Matrix
A matrix is an array of arrays. Here, we create a 4-row by 5-seat matrix where each seat is initially "Empty":
typescriptlet theaterSeats: string[][] = [];
const rows = 4;
const seatsPerRow = 5;

// Initialize the matrix with "Empty" seats
for (let i = 0; i < rows; i++) {
  const row: string[] = [];
  for (let j = 0; j < seatsPerRow; j++) {
    row.push("Empty");
  }
  theaterSeats.push(row);
}

This nested loop fills each row with the correct number of seats and adds it to the matrix.
Modifying Elements
You can update specific seats by accessing them with their row and column indices:
typescript// Reserve seat at Row 0, Seat 2
theaterSeats[0][2] = "Reserved";

// Reserve seats at Row 1, Seat 1 and Seat 3
theaterSeats[1][1] = "Reserved";
theaterSeats[1][3] = "Reserved";

// Reserve seat at Row 3, Seat 4
theaterSeats[3][4] = "Reserved";

Remember, arrays are zero-indexed, so theaterSeats[0][2] refers to the first row, third seat.
Adding Rows
To add a new row of seats, create an array filled with "Empty" and push it to the matrix:
typescriptconst newRow: string[] = Array(seatsPerRow).fill("Empty");
theaterSeats.push(newRow);

This keeps the matrix rectangular, with all rows having the same number of seats.
Visualizing the Matrix
To see the seating arrangement clearly, use a function that prints the matrix row by row:
typescriptfunction printSeating(matrix: string[][]): void {
  console.log("Movie Theater Seating Chart:");
  for (let i = 0; i < matrix.length; i++) {
    console.log(`Row ${i}: ` + matrix[i].join(" | "));
  }
}

printSeating(theaterSeats);

This outputs each row with seat statuses separated by vertical bars for readability.
Practice: Modifying Reservations
Try canceling a reservation by setting a seat back to "Empty":
typescript// Cancel reservation at Row 1, Seat 3
theaterSeats[1][3] = "Empty";

printSeating(theaterSeats);

Important Notes

Maintaining a rectangular matrix is crucial: all rows should have the same number of seats.
Adding or removing columns requires updating every row accordingly.
Direct index access allows precise modification of elements.

Summary

Use nested loops to initialize matrices.
Use .push() to add rows.
Access and modify elements with matrix[row][column] syntax.
Visualize matrices with functions that iterate through rows.

This foundation prepares you for more complex matrix operations and real-world applications.

    03.2 Matrix Iteration and Access
In this lesson, we'll explore how to systematically traverse matrices (2D arrays) using nested loops in TypeScript. We'll analyze a classic example: a tic-tac-toe board, counting the occurrences of each mark and displaying the board clearly.
Understanding Matrix Traversal
A matrix is an array of arrays, where each element is accessed by two indices: the row and the column. To process every element, we use nested loops:

The outer loop iterates over rows.
The inner loop iterates over columns within each row.

This pattern allows us to visit each cell in a row-wise manner.
Example: Tic-Tac-Toe Board
Let's define a 3x3 tic-tac-toe board with some moves:
typescriptconst board: string[][] = [
  ['X', 'O', '-'],
  ['-', 'X', 'O'],
  ['O', '-', 'X'],
];

Here, 'X' and 'O' represent player moves, and '-' indicates an empty space.
Counting Marks with Nested Loops
We want to count how many 'X', 'O', and empty spaces are on the board. Here's how:
typescriptlet countX = 0;
let countO = 0;
let countEmpty = 0;

for (let row = 0; row < board.length; row++) {
  let rowDisplay = '';
  for (let col = 0; col < board[row].length; col++) {
    const cell = board[row][col];
    rowDisplay += cell + ' ';

    if (cell === 'X') {
      countX++;
    } else if (cell === 'O') {
      countO++;
    } else if (cell === '-') {
      countEmpty++;
    }
  }
  console.log(rowDisplay.trim());
}

console.log(`X marks: ${countX}`);
console.log(`O marks: ${countO}`);
console.log(`Empty spaces: ${countEmpty}`);

This code:

Prints each row for visual clarity.
Counts each type of mark.
Uses nested loops to access every cell.

Column-wise Traversal
Sometimes, you may want to process columns instead of rows. For example, counting how many columns contain at least one 'X':
typescriptlet columnsWithX = 0;
for (let col = 0; col < board[0].length; col++) {
  let hasX = false;
  for (let row = 0; row < board.length; row++) {
    if (board[row][col] === 'X') {
      hasX = true;
      break; // Stop checking this column once an 'X' is found
    }
  }
  if (hasX) columnsWithX++;
}
console.log(`Columns containing at least one 'X': ${columnsWithX}`);

Practice Suggestions
Try these exercises to deepen your understanding:

Modify the board by adding more moves and re-run the counts.
Write a function to check if a player has won by completing a row, column, or diagonal.
Experiment with different matrix sizes and contents to generalize your iteration skills.

Key Takeaways

Use nested loops to traverse matrices row-wise or column-wise.
Access elements with matrix[row][column] syntax.
Use break to optimize searches when a condition is met.
Visualizing data during iteration helps understand matrix structure.


Reflect on your learning:
What are the advantages of using nested loops for matrix traversal, and how can you apply this pattern to solve real-world problems involving 2D data structures?

This lesson equips you with the foundational skills to iterate over matrices effectively, preparing you for more advanced data processing tasks.

    04.1 Linear Search in Arrays
Searching through arrays is a fundamental skill in programming, especially when dealing with unsorted data. In this lesson, you'll learn how to implement linear search manually and how to use TypeScript's built-in methods like .find() and .includes() to locate elements efficiently.

What is Linear Search?
Linear search is a simple algorithm that checks each element in an array sequentially until it finds the target value or reaches the end of the array.
Manual Linear Search Example
typescriptfunction linearSearch(arr: string[], target: string): number {
  for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    if (arr[i] === target) {
      return i; // Found target at index i
    }
  }
  return -1; // Target not found
}

const students: string[] = ["Ana", "Bob", "Carlos", "Diana", "Eva"];
const searchName = "Carlos";
const index = linearSearch(students, searchName);

if (index !== -1) {
  console.log(`${searchName} found at index ${index}`);
} else {
  console.log(`${searchName} not found in the list.`);
}

This function returns the index of the target if found, or -1 if not.

Using .find() to Locate Objects
When working with arrays of objects, .find() helps locate the first element that matches a condition.
typescriptinterface Student {
  name: string;
  grade: number;
}

const studentObjects: Student[] = [
  { name: "Ana", grade: 85 },
  { name: "Bob", grade: 92 },
  { name: "Carlos", grade: 78 },
];

const topStudent = studentObjects.find(student => student.grade > 90);

if (topStudent) {
  console.log(`Top student: ${topStudent.name} with grade ${topStudent.grade}`);
} else {
  console.log("No student found with grade above 90.");
}

.find() returns the first matching object or undefined if none match.

Checking Existence with .includes()
To check if an array contains a specific value, use .includes(), which returns a boolean.
typescriptconst hasEva = students.includes("Eva");
console.log(`Is Eva in the list? ${hasEva}`); // true


Practice Opportunity
Try these tasks to solidify your understanding:

Modify the linearSearch function to return the student object instead of the index.
Use .find() to locate a student by exact name.
Use .includes() to check if a grade exists in an array of grades.

Experimenting with these will deepen your grasp of searching techniques in TypeScript arrays.

Mastering these search methods will empower you to efficiently locate data in arrays, a crucial skill for real-world programming challenges.

    InstructionsCode04.2 Binary Search Algorithm
Binary search is a powerful algorithm used to find the position of a target value within a sorted array. Unlike linear search, which checks each element one by one, binary search efficiently narrows down the search space by repeatedly dividing the array in half.
How Binary Search Works

Start with two pointers: low at the beginning of the array and high at the end.
Calculate the middle index between low and high.
Compare the middle element with the target:

If they are equal, you've found the target!
If the middle element is less than the target, move low to mid + 1 to search the right half.
If the middle element is greater than the target, move high to mid - 1 to search the left half.


Repeat steps 2-3 until the target is found or the search space is empty (low > high).

Why Use Binary Search?

Efficiency: Binary search runs in O(log n) time, much faster than linear search's O(n), especially for large arrays.
Requirement: The array must be sorted for binary search to work correctly.

Binary Search Implementation in TypeScript
typescriptfunction binarySearch(arr: number[], target: number): number {
  let low = 0; // Start index
  let high = arr.length - 1; // End index

  while (low <= high) {
    // Calculate middle index to avoid overflow
    let mid = Math.floor(low + (high - low) / 2);

    if (arr[mid] === target) {
      return mid; // Found target, return index
    } else if (arr[mid] < target) {
      low = mid + 1; // Search right half
    } else {
      high = mid - 1; // Search left half
    }
  }

  return -1; // Target not found
}

// Example usage
const sortedNumbers = [3, 8, 15, 23, 42, 56, 78, 91];

console.log(binarySearch(sortedNumbers, 42)); // Output: 4
console.log(binarySearch(sortedNumbers, 50)); // Output: -1

Visualizing Binary Search

Practice Challenge
Try searching for different numbers in the sortedNumbers array. What happens if you search for the first or last element? What if the array is empty or has only one element? Experiment by modifying the array and target values to observe how the algorithm behaves.

    04.3 Common Array Pitfalls
Working with arrays is fundamental in programming, but certain common mistakes can lead to bugs and unexpected behavior. In this lesson, we'll explore frequent pitfalls when handling arrays in TypeScript and learn how to avoid them with best practices.

Pitfall 1: Hardcoding Array Length
Avoid using fixed numbers when iterating over arrays. Hardcoding the length can cause your code to break if the array size changes.
typescript// ❌ Problematic: fixed limit
let tweets = ["Hello", "World", "TypeScript"];
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { // What if tweets grows?
  console.log(tweets[i]);
}

// ✅ Correct: use .length property
for (let i = 0; i < tweets.length; i++) {
  console.log(tweets[i]);
}

Using .length ensures your loop adapts dynamically to the array size.

Pitfall 2: Mutating Array During Iteration
Removing or adding elements while iterating forward can cause elements to be skipped or processed multiple times.
typescript// ❌ Problematic: removing while looping forward
let notifications = ["like", "comment", "follow", "share"];
for (let i = 0; i < notifications.length; i++) {
  if (notifications[i] === "comment") {
    notifications.splice(i, 1); // removes "comment"
    // Next element shifts left, but i increments, skipping it
  }
}
console.log(notifications); // Unexpected result

// ✅ Correct: iterate backwards when removing
let notifications = ["like", "comment", "follow", "share"];
for (let i = notifications.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
  if (notifications[i] === "comment") {
    notifications.splice(i, 1);
  }
}
console.log(notifications); // Correctly removed

Iterating backwards prevents skipping elements because the array shifts don't affect unvisited indices.

Pitfall 3: Accessing Out-of-Bounds Indices
Accessing indices outside the array range returns undefined silently, which can cause bugs if unchecked.
typescript// ❌ Problematic: no bounds check
let feed = ["post1", "post2"];
console.log(feed[5]); // undefined, no error but unexpected

// ✅ Correct: check bounds before access
let index = 5;
if (index >= 0 && index < feed.length) {
  console.log(feed[index]);
} else {
  console.log("Index out of range");
}

Always verify indices before accessing array elements to avoid unexpected undefined values.

Pitfall 4: Mixing Types in Arrays
Arrays should be homogeneous in TypeScript to maintain clarity and type safety. Mixing types leads to confusing code and runtime errors.
typescript// ❌ Problematic: mixed types
let mixed = ["text", 42, true];

// ✅ Correct: use typed arrays
let messages: string[] = ["Hello", "World"];
let counts: number[] = [1, 2, 3];

Declaring explicit array types helps the compiler catch errors and improves code readability.

Defensive Programming Tips

Always use .length for loops instead of hardcoded numbers.
When removing elements during iteration, loop backwards or collect indices to remove after.
Check array bounds before accessing elements.
Declare array types explicitly in TypeScript.


Visual Summary


Practice Tip
Try refactoring a social media sidebar array to avoid these pitfalls. For example, ensure your notifications array only contains strings, iterate using .length, and avoid modifying the array while looping forward. This approach prevents bugs and makes your code easier to maintain and extend.

By recognizing and avoiding these common pitfalls, you'll write more reliable and maintainable array code in TypeScript. Keep these best practices in mind as you continue your journey mastering arrays!

    InstructionsCode04.4 Searching in Matrices
Searching for values in two-dimensional arrays, or matrices, is a fundamental skill in programming. Whether you're building a game board, analyzing data grids, or managing seating charts, knowing how to locate elements efficiently is essential.
Understanding Matrix Search
A matrix is essentially an array of arrays. To search for a value, you need to check each element in every row and column. This requires nested loops: an outer loop to iterate over rows, and an inner loop to iterate over columns within each row.
Key Concepts

Outer loop iterates over each row (index i).
Inner loop iterates over each column in the current row (index j).
When the target value is found, return its position as an object { row: i, col: j }.
If the target is not found, return null.

Example: Finding the First Occurrence
typescriptfunction findInMatrix(matrix: number[][], target: number): { row: number; col: number } | null {
  for (let row = 0; row < matrix.length; row++) {
    for (let col = 0; col < matrix[row].length; col++) {
      if (matrix[row][col] === target) {
        // Return position as an object when found
        return { row, col };
      }
    }
  }
  // Return null if target not found
  return null;
}

This function stops searching as soon as it finds the first match, which is efficient when you only need one occurrence.
Example: Finding All Occurrences
Sometimes, you need to find every position where the target appears. For this, collect all matching positions in an array.
typescriptfunction findAllInMatrix(matrix: number[][], target: number): { row: number; col: number }[] {
  const positions: { row: number; col: number }[] = [];
  for (let row = 0; row < matrix.length; row++) {
    for (let col = 0; col < matrix[row].length; col++) {
      if (matrix[row][col] === target) {
        positions.push({ row, col });
      }
    }
  }
  return positions;
}

This function checks every element and returns an array of all positions where the target is found.
Practical Example: Treasure Hunt Grid
Imagine a 5x5 grid representing a treasure map with numbers indicating treasures.
typescriptconst treasureGrid = [
  [5, 3, 7, 1, 9],
  [2, 8, 3, 4, 6],
  [9, 3, 5, 7, 2],
  [1, 6, 8, 3, 4],
  [7, 2, 9, 5, 3],
];

const firstTreasure = findInMatrix(treasureGrid, 3);
console.log('First treasure found at:', firstTreasure); // { row: 0, col: 1 }

const allTreasures = findAllInMatrix(treasureGrid, 3);
console.log('All treasures found at:', allTreasures);

Why Return Positions as Objects?
Returning positions as objects with row and col properties makes it easy to integrate with user interfaces, such as highlighting cells in a game board or spreadsheet.

    05.0 Array Manipulation Challenges
Mastering arrays means not only knowing individual methods but also combining them effectively to solve real-world problems. In this lesson, we'll explore how to tackle complex array manipulation challenges by chaining operations like map, filter, reduce, and sort. These skills empower you to process data such as student grades, inventory lists, and matrices with precision and clarity.
Why Combine Array Methods?
Each array method serves a specific purpose:

map() transforms each element.
filter() selects elements based on conditions.
reduce() aggregates values into a single result.
sort() orders elements.

By combining these, you can build powerful data pipelines that are both readable and efficient.
Example Challenge: Student Grade Processing
Imagine you have an array of student objects with their scores:
typescriptlet students = [
  { name: "Ana", scores: [85, 90, 78] },
  { name: "Bob", scores: [92, 88, 95] },
  { name: "Carlos", scores: [76, 84, 89] },
];

Tasks:

Calculate each student's average score.
Create a new array with student names and their averages.
Sort students by average score in descending order.
Filter students with averages of 85 or higher.
Print the honor roll.

This sequence uses map to calculate averages, sort to order students, and filter to select top performers.
Example Challenge: Inventory Management
Given a product inventory:
typescriptlet inventory = [
  { product: "Laptop", quantity: 5, price: 999 },
  { product: "Mouse", quantity: 25, price: 25 },
  { product: "Keyboard", quantity: 15, price: 75 },
];

Tasks:

Calculate total inventory value (quantity × price).
Find the most expensive product.
Filter products with quantity less than 10.
Sort products by quantity ascending.
Create a restock list for low quantity items.

This challenge combines map, reduce, filter, and sort to manage inventory data.
Example Challenge: Matrix Operations
Work with a 4x4 matrix of numbers 1 through 16:

Calculate the sum of each row.
Calculate the sum of each column.
Find the maximum value in the matrix.
Count how many numbers are even.

This requires nested loops and aggregation techniques.

Put your knowledge to the test!
Select the correct answer for each question.
Which array method would you use to create a new array with transformed elements without modifying the original? filter() map() reduce() sort()What does the filter() method return? A single value A new array with elements that meet the condition The original array modified The index of the first matching elementWhen combining array methods, which order is generally correct to first select, then transform, then aggregate? map() → filter() → reduce() reduce() → map() → filter() filter() → map() → reduce() sort() → reduce() → map()In the inventory example, which method helps calculate the total value of all products? map() filter() reduce() sort()What is a key benefit of chaining array methods? It makes code longer and harder to read It creates clear, readable data processing pipelines It always improves performance It avoids the need for loops entirelyHow would you find the maximum value in a matrix? Use a single reduce() on the matrix Use map() to flatten the matrix Use nested loops to compare each element Use filter() to select the maxWhat does the sort() method do to the original array? Returns a new sorted array without changing the original Sorts the original array in place (mutates it) Does not change the array Throws an error if the array is empty
Ask Rigo how to combine array methods effectively

By mastering these challenges, you build confidence to handle complex data transformations and prepare for more advanced programming concepts ahead.

    InstructionsCode05.1 RealWorld Array Problems
Let's dive into a practical example that demonstrates how to apply multiple array methods together to solve a common programming task: processing an e-commerce shopping cart. This example will show you how to transform, filter, sort, and aggregate data efficiently using TypeScript.

E-commerce Shopping Cart Processing
Imagine you have a shopping cart represented as an array of product objects. Each product has a name, price, and quantity.
typescriptlet cart = [
  { name: "Laptop", price: 1200, quantity: 1 },
  { name: "Headphones", price: 100, quantity: 2 },
  { name: "Mouse", price: 50, quantity: 1 },
  { name: "Keyboard", price: 80, quantity: 0 }, // out of stock
];

Step 1: Calculate total price per item
Use the .map() method to create a new array containing the total price for each item (price multiplied by quantity).
typescriptlet itemTotals = cart.map(item => item.price * item.quantity);
console.log(itemTotals); // [1200, 200, 50, 0]

Step 2: Calculate the total cart value
Use .reduce() to sum all the item totals into a single cart total.
typescriptlet cartTotal = itemTotals.reduce((sum, current) => sum + current, 0);
console.log(`Cart Total: $${cartTotal}`); // Cart Total: $1450

Step 3: Apply a discount to expensive items
Use .map() again to apply a 10% discount to items priced over $100.
typescriptlet discountedCart = cart.map(item => {
  if (item.price > 100) {
    return { ...item, price: item.price * 0.9 };
  }
  return item;
});

Step 4: Remove out-of-stock items
Use .filter() to exclude items with zero quantity.
typescriptlet filteredCart = discountedCart.filter(item => item.quantity > 0);

Step 5: Sort items by total value descending
Sort the filtered cart so the most valuable items appear first.
typescriptfilteredCart.sort((a, b) => (b.price * b.quantity) - (a.price * a.quantity));

Step 6: Print the final cart summary
Use .forEach() to display each item's details and the final total.
typescriptfilteredCart.forEach(item => {
  console.log(`${item.name}: $${item.price.toFixed(2)} x ${item.quantity} = $${(item.price * item.quantity).toFixed(2)}`);
});

let finalTotal = filteredCart.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.quantity, 0);
console.log(`Total Cart Value: $${finalTotal.toFixed(2)}`);


Why This Matters
This pattern of chaining array methods allows you to write clear, maintainable, and adaptable code for complex data transformations. Whether managing inventories, processing orders, or analyzing datasets, these techniques are essential.

Practice Challenge
Try modifying the cart:

Add a new product with a different price and quantity.
Change the discount threshold or percentage.
Update quantities and observe how the final output changes.

Experimenting with these changes will deepen your understanding of array method chaining.

    05.2 Arrays Knowledge Test
Let's put your understanding of TypeScript arrays to the test! Answer the following multiple-choice questions to evaluate your grasp of array fundamentals, methods, iteration, and searching techniques.
1. After these operations, what will be logged?
typescriptlet numbers: number[] = [10, 20, 30];
numbers.push(40);
numbers.unshift(5);
console.log(numbers[2]);

After these operations, what will be logged? A) 10 B) 20 C) 30 D) 40
Explanation: After push(40), the array becomes [10, 20, 30, 40]. Then unshift(5) adds 5 at the start, resulting in [5, 10, 20, 30, 40]. Index 2 is 20.

2. Which method returns a boolean indicating if an array contains a specific value?
Which method returns a boolean indicating if an array contains a specific value? A) .indexOf() B) .includes() C) .find() D) .filter()
Explanation: .includes() returns true or false depending on whether the element exists. .indexOf() returns the index or -1.

3. What is the output of this code?
typescriptlet values = [2, 4, 6, 8];
let result = values.map(x => x * 2);
console.log(values.length === result.length);

What is the output of this code? A) true B) false C) undefined D) Error
Explanation: .map() creates a new array with the same length as the original, transforming each element.

4. Given the matrix:
typescriptlet grid = [
  [1, 2, 3],
  [4, 5, 6],
  [7, 8, 9],
];

What is grid[2][0]?
What is grid[2][0]? A) 3 B) 6 C) 7 D) 9
Explanation: grid[2] is the third row [7, 8, 9], and [0] is the first element of that row, which is 7.

5. What is wrong with this code?
typescriptlet nums = [100, 20, 3];
nums.sort();
console.log(nums);

What is wrong with this code? A) Nothing, it works correctly B) .sort() without comparison treats numbers as strings C) .sort() doesn't modify the original array D) .sort() requires two parameters
Explanation: Without a comparison function, .sort() converts numbers to strings and sorts lexicographically, leading to incorrect order.

6. Binary search requires:
Binary search requires: A) Any array B) A sorted array C) An array with unique values D) An array with less than 100 elements
Explanation: Binary search only works correctly on sorted arrays because it divides the search space in half each step.

7. Which is the correct way to iterate through an array?
Which is the correct way to iterate through an array? A) for (let i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++) B) for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) C) for (let i = 1; i <= arr.length; i++) D) while (true) { arr[i]; i++; }
Explanation: The loop should start at 0 and run while i is less than arr.length to avoid out-of-bounds access.

Great job! Review any questions you found challenging and revisit the lessons to strengthen your understanding of arrays in TypeScript.

    06.0 Conclusion and Next Steps
You've now mastered one of the fundamental building blocks of programming: arrays. Throughout this course, you've learned how to create, access, and manipulate arrays in TypeScript, explored iteration techniques, worked with multi-dimensional matrices, and applied searching and sorting algorithms to solve practical problems.
What You've Accomplished

Created and modified arrays using literal notation and array methods.
Traversed arrays with loops and modern iteration methods like .forEach(), .map(), and .filter().
Handled multi-dimensional arrays (matrices) with nested loops and understood their real-world applications.
Implemented searching algorithms, including linear and binary search.
Applied sorting techniques with .sort() and custom comparison functions.
Recognized and avoided common pitfalls when working with arrays.

These skills form a solid foundation for managing collections of data efficiently and effectively in your programs.
Looking Ahead: Objects and Beyond
Arrays are powerful, but real-world data often requires more complex structures. The next step in your journey is to learn about objects — data structures that group related properties and values by meaning rather than position. Combining arrays and objects will enable you to model complex entities like users, products, and more.
The iteration and searching patterns you've mastered with arrays will also apply to objects, making this transition smoother.
Keep Practicing and Building
To deepen your understanding and prepare for the next topics, consider:

Solving additional array challenges on coding platforms.
Refactoring your code to use modern array methods.
Building mini-projects like a todo list, grade calculator, or inventory system.

Reflect and Share
In your own words, describe what you have learned about arrays in this course and how you plan to apply these skills in your programming projects.

Keep up the great work! You're ready to explore objects and take your programming skills to the next level.
